claims.text: Skidmore and Fitts compiled publicly reported unsupported journal voucher adjustments from OIG and GAO documents for FY1998-FY2015 and arrived at roughly $21 trillion for DoD and roughly $350 billion for HUD.

The authors state: 'The Inspector General's reports that are available to the public only provide summary information; thus it is impossible for us to conduct a detailed assessment of the nature of these unsupported adjustments and errors.'
The authors state they were unable to recover data for a number of years within the FY1998-FY2015 window.

The $21 trillion figure double-counts by construction, because gross adjustment volumes across eighteen years are being summed and individual dollars are adjusted repeatedly; it is an index of documentation failure, not a quantity of money. Reasoning: it is derived from the same class of gross-entry figures as the DODIG-2016-113 $6.5 trillion number, which the OIG itself flags as non-cumulative.

desc: Mark Skidmore, an economist at Michigan State University, and Catherine Austin Fitts, a former Assistant Secretary of Housing at HUD and former managing director at Dillon Read, compiled the unsupported journal voucher adjustment figures reported in publicly available Inspector General and Government Accountability Office documents for the Department of Defense and the Department of Housing and Urban Development across fiscal years 1998 to 2015. Their summary report, dated September 2017, arrives at approximately $21 trillion for DoD and approximately $350 billion for HUD. The figure is a sum of gross adjustment amounts drawn from summary tables in OIG reports; the authors state explicitly that 'The Inspector General's reports that are available to the public only provide summary information; thus it is impossible for us to conduct a detailed assessment of the nature of these unsupported adjustments and errors', and that data could not be recovered for a number of years. The number is therefore not a measure of money that went missing, was stolen, or was spent off-book, and the authors do not claim that it is. What it is, and what makes it usable, is an aggregate index of the scale at which two cabinet departments made accounting entries they could not document, sustained over eighteen years and across administrations of both parties. The figure has been repeatedly and damagingly overstated in secondary coverage as '$21 trillion missing'; that formulation is indefensible and should never be used on this board. The defensible formulation is: over eighteen fiscal years, DoD and HUD made publicly reported unsupported adjustments whose gross value totalled roughly $21 trillion, and neither department can say what those entries were for.

The authors state that the public reports 'only provide summary information; thus it is impossible for us to conduct a detailed assessment of the nature of these unsupported adjustments and errors'.
